title: XVAE-WMT: Explainable Wavelet-Temporal Variational Autoencoder for Blind Source Separation of Heart and Lung Sounds
summary: The separation of cardiovascular sounds is a critical task in biomedical signal processing. In this paper, we introduce XVAE-WMT1, an unsupervised explainable generative AI algorithm combining a variational autoencoder (VAE) with explainable AI (XAI), wavelet-based inputs, a post-hoc output mask, and temporal consistency (TC) loss. Unlike existing supervised and VAE-based methods that rely on Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and ignore latent interpretability, XVAE-WMT requires no paired clean recordings and integrates a Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) front-end for superior time-frequency localization. We assessed the latent space interpretability via different metrics, with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) enabling dimensionality reduction to the top 75% of latent features while preserving separation quality. Evaluated across two datasets using Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SDR), Signal-to-Interference Ratio (SIR), and Signal-to-Artifacts Ratio (SAR), XVAE-WMT attains 26.8 dB SDR, 32.8 dB SIR, and 28.6 dB SAR.

AI.tldr: XVAE-WMT1 is an unsupervised explainable AI algorithm for cardiovascular sound separation, combining VAE with XAI, wavelet transforms, and temporal consistency loss. It achieves state-of-the-art performance (26.8 dB SDR, 32.8 dB SIR, 28.6 dB SAR) without requiring paired clean recordings.
AI.motivation: Existing supervised and VAE-based methods for cardiovascular sound separation rely on Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and ignore latent interpretability. This paper addresses the need for unsupervised methods that work without paired clean recordings while providing interpretable latent spaces.
AI.method: XVAE-WMT1 integrates: (1) a variational autoencoder (VAE) backbone, (2) explainable AI (XAI) for latent interpretability, (3) Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) front-end for superior time-frequency localization, (4) a post-hoc output mask, and (5) temporal consistency (TC) loss. SHAP analysis enables dimensionality reduction to top 75% of latent features while preserving separation quality.
AI.result: Evaluated across two datasets using SDR, SIR, and SAR metrics, XVAE-WMT1 achieves 26.8 dB SDR, 32.8 dB SIR, and 28.6 dB SAR, demonstrating superior separation performance.
AI.conclusion: XVAE-WMT1 successfully combines unsupervised learning with explainability, achieving high-quality cardiovascular sound separation without paired clean recordings. The SHAP-enabled latent space interpretability allows dimensionality reduction while maintaining performance, making the model both effective and interpretable.

title: Cleaner Speech, Weaker Generalization: Revisiting Pitt-Derived Benchmarks for Alzheimer's Disease Detection
summary: Speech-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection increasingly relies on speech-enhanced and curated versions of the Pitt Corpus, where speech enhancement, sample selection, and demographic balancing are often treated as beneficial preprocessing steps. However, whether these transformations improve real-world AD detection or instead affect model generalization and prediction behavior remains unclear. In this work, we revisit the role of speech preprocessing and dataset curation across widely used benchmarks for speech-based AD detection. We evaluate the speech quality of different datasets, the cross-dataset generalization of multiple deep learning models under matched and mismatched enhancement settings, and the behavior of several recent large audio-language models (LALMs). Experimental results show that across multiple supervised speech models, speech-enhanced datasets often improve in-domain performance while reducing robustness in cross-domain evaluation. Matched enhancement between training and test data alleviates, but does not eliminate, this degradation. LALMs show a similar sensitivity: enhanced datasets induce stronger class imbalance and prediction shifts than unprocessed data. These results suggest that speech preprocessing and dataset curation can substantially influence downstream AD detection behavior, indicating that ``cleaner'' speech datasets are not necessarily more reliable for real-world AD detection.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether speech preprocessing (enhancement, sample selection, demographic balancing) improves or harms real-world Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection. The study evaluates multiple datasets, deep learning models, and large audio-language models (LALMs) under matched and mismatched enhancement settings.
AI.motivation: Speech-based AD detection relies on preprocessed versions of the Pitt Corpus, but it remains unclear whether these transformations improve real-world detection or affect model generalization and prediction behavior.
AI.method: Evaluated speech quality across datasets; tested cross-dataset generalization of multiple deep learning models under matched/mismatched enhancement settings; analyzed behavior of several recent large audio-language models (LALMs).
AI.result: Speech-enhanced datasets improve in-domain performance but reduce robustness in cross-domain evaluation. Matched enhancement alleviates but does not eliminate this degradation. LALMs show similar sensitivity, with enhanced datasets inducing stronger class imbalance and prediction shifts than unprocessed data.
AI.conclusion: Speech preprocessing and dataset curation substantially influence downstream AD detection behavior. 'Cleaner' speech datasets are not necessarily more reliable for real-world AD detection.

title: BiMTokenizer: Preserving Semantic-Acoustic Balance in Low-Bitrate Speech Tokenization via Bidirectional State-Space Modeling
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference; 19 pages, 5 figures
summary: Speech codecs serve as bridges between continuous speech signals and large language models, yet face an inherent conflict between acoustic fidelity and semantic preservation. To mitigate this conflict, recent works increasingly adopt dual-tower architectures to decouple semantic and acoustic modeling with separate encoders. However, these dual-tower designs incur substantial architectural overhead. To avoid such complexity, we revisit the single-tower paradigm and propose BiMTokenizer, a low-bitrate speech codec (around 1.1 kbps) combining a bidirectional state-space backbone with Residual Spherical Leech Quantization (RSLQ). The bidirectional backbone strengthens temporal modeling, while RSLQ offers a fixed, well-separated lattice bottleneck for robust semantic and acoustic tokenization without learned-codebook collapse. Experiments show that BiMTokenizer achieves superior acoustic reconstruction and the lowest WER among low-bitrate codec baselines across both clean and noisy environments, while using less than half the parameters of recent dual-tower baselines. Furthermore, its robust semantic representations yield strong performance on downstream speech understanding tasks, confirming that a well-designed single-tower codec can preserve the semantic-acoustic balance at low bitrates. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/ZhangXinWhut/BiMTokenizer.

AI.tldr: BiMTokenizer is a low-bitrate speech codec (1.1 kbps) that uses a bidirectional state-space backbone with Residual Spherical Leech Quantization (RSLQ) to balance semantic and acoustic modeling in a single-tower architecture, avoiding the complexity of dual-tower designs.
AI.motivation: Speech codecs face an inherent conflict between acoustic fidelity and semantic preservation. Recent dual-tower architectures decouple semantic and acoustic modeling but incur substantial architectural overhead. This work aims to achieve similar or better performance with a simpler single-tower design.
AI.method: BiMTokenizer combines: (1) A bidirectional state-space backbone for strengthened temporal modeling, and (2) Residual Spherical Leech Quantization (RSLQ) providing a fixed, well-separated lattice bottleneck for robust semantic and acoustic tokenization without learned-codebook collapse.
AI.result: BiMTokenizer achieves superior acoustic reconstruction and the lowest WER among low-bitrate codec baselines across both clean and noisy environments, while using less than half the parameters of recent dual-tower baselines. It also yields strong performance on downstream speech understanding tasks.
AI.conclusion: A well-designed single-tower codec can preserve the semantic-acoustic balance at low bitrates, achieving state-of-the-art results with significantly fewer parameters than dual-tower approaches.

title: TUTTI: Toward generalizable audio-to-score transcription via fully synthesized data
summary: Generalizable Audio-to-Score (A2S) transcription is fundamentally constrained by the severe scarcity of high-quality, real-world paired data. Relying solely on existing human-annotated datasets often restricts the generalization of A2S models, limiting their efficacy primarily to single-instrumentation domains. To break this dependency on scarce real-world data, we introduce TUTTI (Transformer for Unified audio-To-score Transcription trained on Synthetic multi-Instrumentation Data), a pre-training paradigm driven by a purely synthetic, large-scale dataset. Rather than using human-composed scores, we leverage a symbolic music generation model to generate a massive, highly scalable multi-instrumentation corpus and create audio-score pairs with expressive acoustic characteristics. Capitalizing on the generated data, we employ a standard Transformer encoder-decoder architecture. We empirically demonstrate that pre-training a unified attention-based model on generated, multi-instrumentation data yields a consistently stronger foundational representation than single-instrumentation training. When fine-tuned with downstream real-world datasets, TUTTI outperforms previous approaches, establishing new overall state-of-the-art results across various A2S baselines. Notably, TUTTI shows remarkable cross-instrument transferability, effectively adapting to unseen instruments with highly competitive performance. The source code and the TuttiCorpus dataset will be made publicly available at https://github.com/a-musiclover/TUTTI.

AI.tldr: TUTTI is a pre-training paradigm for Audio-to-Score transcription that uses synthetic multi-instrumentation data generated by a symbolic music model, eliminating dependence on scarce real-world annotated data. It employs a Transformer encoder-decoder architecture and achieves state-of-the-art results with strong cross-instrument transferability.
AI.motivation: A2S transcription is constrained by severe scarcity of high-quality real-world paired data, limiting models to single-instrumentation domains and poor generalization.
AI.method: Uses a symbolic music generation model to create a large-scale multi-instrumentation corpus (TuttiCorpus), generates audio-score pairs with expressive acoustic characteristics, and pre-trains a unified Transformer encoder-decoder model on this synthetic data before fine-tuning on real-world datasets.
AI.result: Pre-training on multi-instrumentation data yields stronger foundational representations than single-instrumentation training. TUTTI establishes new state-of-the-art results across various A2S baselines and shows remarkable cross-instrument transferability, adapting effectively to unseen instruments.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data generation is a viable solution to break the dependency on scarce real-world data in A2S transcription, enabling effective cross-instrument generalization and establishing new performance benchmarks.

title: Task-Specific Prompt with Global Context for Multi-Task Graph Pre-Training
summary: Graph prompt learning is an effective paradigm to adapt pre-trained graph models to downstream tasks in low-resource scenarios. However, existing multi-task graph pre-training frameworks generally use randomly initialized prompts, leading to poor alignment between the prompt space, pretext objectives and graph structural characteristics. This greatly weakens the task relevance, structural awareness and transferability of prompt representations. To address this challenge, we propose TPGC, a dual-prior prompt initialization solution that explicitly models the synergy between task prior and structural prior. Specifically, the Task-Prior Injection Module first conducts a short homologous multi-task pre-training on an auxiliary graph, enabling prompt initialization to inherit optimization preferences associated with multiple pretext tasks. Built on the task-aware representations, the Structure-Prior Injection Module further extracts transferable global structural context from the auxiliary graph, converting it into layer-wise prompt vectors by aggregating structurally informative node embeddings. Extensive experiments on 6 mainstream benchmarks covering node and graph classification show that TPGC achieves consistently better performance under few-shot settings than state-of-the-art baselines, with fewer downstream tunable parameters and lower runtime. The code is available at https://github.com/Virgilqiu/TPGC

AI.tldr: TPGC proposes a dual-prior prompt initialization solution for graph prompt learning that addresses the poor alignment issue in existing methods by explicitly modeling task prior and structural prior through two specialized modules.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-task graph pre-training frameworks use randomly initialized prompts, leading to poor alignment between prompt space, pretext objectives, and graph structural characteristics. This weakens task relevance, structural awareness, and transferability of prompt representations.
AI.method: TPGC introduces two modules: (1) Task-Prior Injection Module conducts short homologous multi-task pre-training on an auxiliary graph to enable prompt initialization to inherit optimization preferences from multiple pretext tasks; (2) Structure-Prior Injection Module extracts transferable global structural context from the auxiliary graph and converts it into layer-wise prompt vectors by aggregating structurally informative node embeddings.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 6 mainstream benchmarks covering node and graph classification show that TPGC achieves consistently better performance under few-shot settings than state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: TPGC achieves superior performance with fewer downstream tunable parameters and lower runtime compared to SOTA baselines, effectively addressing the alignment problem in graph prompt learning.

title: Can LLMs Design Video Coding Tools? A Case Study on Planar Mode
summary: This paper explores whether large language models (LLMs) can design video coding tools, a highly challenging task due to the intricate algorithmic coupling of tool modifications. In particular, we present an empirical case study on the Planar mode, a long-standing intra prediction tool in video coding standards. Our experiments operate within a generation-and-evaluation loop, with the LLM generating new Planar predictors, encoder trials evaluating their coding performance, and the LLM re-generating refined implementations based on the evaluation feedback. We first examine directly replacing the default Planar mode in the Fraunhofer Versatile Video Encoder (VVenC) under its faster preset. Experimental results demonstrate that the LLM-generated mode can outperform the conventional Planar mode on this lightweight toolset, achieving 0.18% bitrate savings with 0.4% complexity overhead on the standard benchmark. We further extend our evaluation to the Enhanced Compression Model (ECM). Leveraging newly introduced directional Planar modes, we investigate two integration strategies: directly replacing them, and introducing the LLM-generated predictor as an additional prediction mode with new syntax elements. The empirical results suggest that both strategies can yield coding gains under a constrained low-resolution setting. Overall, this study offers preliminary evidence and practical insights, highlighting both the potential and open challenges of LLM-based coding tool design.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models can design video coding tools, using the Planar intra prediction mode as a case study. Through a generation-and-evaluation loop, the LLM generates new Planar predictors, which are evaluated by the encoder, and the LLM refines based on feedback. Results show 0.18% bitrate savings with 0.4% complexity overhead in VVenC, and coding gains in ECM under low-resolution settings.
AI.motivation: Explore whether large language models can design video coding tools, which is a highly challenging task due to the intricate algorithmic coupling of tool modifications.
AI.method: Empirical case study on Planar mode (a long-standing intra prediction tool in video coding standards). Uses a generation-and-evaluation loop where: (1) LLM generates new Planar predictors, (2) encoder evaluates their coding performance, (3) LLM refines implementations based on evaluation feedback. Experiments on VVenC (faster preset) and ECM (with directional Planar modes), testing two integration strategies: direct replacement and adding as new prediction mode with new syntax elements.
AI.result: 1. VVenC (faster preset): LLM-generated mode outperforms conventional Planar mode by 0.18% bitrate savings with 0.4% complexity overhead on standard benchmark. 2. ECM: Both integration strategies (direct replacement and additional mode) yield coding gains under constrained low-resolution setting.
AI.conclusion: The study offers preliminary evidence and practical insights, highlighting both the potential and open challenges of LLM-based coding tool design.

title: Inverse Rendering for Modeling with Line Primitives
summary: Faithfully capturing diverse real-world objects with fuzzy, anisotropic structures, such as hair, fur, fibers, and textiles, for efficient real-time visualization remains challenging. Recent radiance field reconstruction methods capture these structures from multi-view images using translucent volumetric primitives such as 3D Gaussians rather than opaque low-dimensional primitives (e.g., triangles, line segments, and polylines), thereby limiting compatibility with standard depth-tested rasterization, reflection modeling, and physical simulation. We present an inverse rendering method for reconstructing fuzzy geometry using explicit line segments, which are rasterized on a subpixel grid for anti-aliasing to reproduce a semi-transparent appearance. While straightforward to render, optimizing numerous line primitives to match target images poses a significant challenge. We address this by introducing a stochastic differentiable rasterizer for line segments that produces informative gradients with respect to vertex positions, attributes, and discrete connectivity. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method outperforms surface-based approaches in capturing fuzzy boundaries and achieves quality comparable to volumetric representations while relying entirely on explicit geometry. The resulting representation integrates seamlessly with standard graphics pipelines, enabling cross-platform rendering, various shading models, and physical simulation.

title: Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents -- A Source-Code Study of Eleven Systems
comment: 83 pages, 7 figures, 18 tables. Second, substantially expanded edition of an April 2026 study: corpus grown from eight to eleven systems plus a meta-harness contrast point; the retained April snapshots provide a controlled longitudinal comparison
summary: An agent is a model plus a harness -- the runtime that couples an LLM to the world through a loop, tools, context management, safety controls, orchestration, and extension surfaces. Harness engineering, named as a discipline in early 2026, is the design and evolution of that runtime. This paper gives the young discipline its most comprehensive empirical foundation to date: a source-code anatomy of eleven production coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe, OpenHands, Aider, Mini-SWE-Agent, Hermes, Pi, OpenCode, OpenClaw), plus Omnigent, the first meta-harness, analyzed as a contrast point. We define what a harness is, map its seven canonical subsystems with the minimal and maximal implementation of each, and dissect all eleven systems along those subsystems. The audit yields 13 cross-cutting observations and a catalog of 29 recurring design patterns. Two absences survive a threefold corpus expansion: across roughly four million lines of Python, TypeScript, and Rust, no agent runtime imports a general-purpose agentic framework, and none retrieves code with vector embeddings; the field runs on hand-rolled async loops and deterministic retrieval. SKILL.md skills lead MCP in adoption (9/11 vs. 8/11), and ACP ships in six systems with a new third role: harness hosting. Because the original eight systems were re-pinned rather than replaced, the study also contains a controlled longitudinal sample -- the same harnesses source-diffed across one quarter -- showing convergence becoming imitation and behavioral policy migrating from prompt prose to configuration. These threads converge on the paper's thesis: in the first half of 2026 the coding harness completed a turn from tool to platform. The paper closes with 18 design recommendations and a 90-line minimum-viable-harness scaffold.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes harness engineering as a new discipline by providing the first comprehensive empirical analysis of 11 production coding agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, etc.) plus a meta-harness. Through source-code analysis of ~4 million lines across Python, TypeScript, and Rust, the study maps seven canonical subsystems, identifies 13 cross-cutting observations and 29 recurring design patterns, and documents two significant absences: no use of general-purpose agentic frameworks and no vector embedding-based code retrieval.
AI.motivation: To provide the young discipline of harness engineering with its first comprehensive empirical foundation by systematically analyzing production coding agent runtimes through source-code anatomy, addressing the gap between the rapid adoption of agent systems and the lack of rigorous understanding of their architectural patterns and design choices.
AI.method: Source-code anatomy of eleven production coding harnesses plus one meta-harness (Omnigent), mapping each against seven defined canonical subsystems with minimal/maximal implementations. The study includes a controlled longitudinal sample comparing the same harnesses across one quarter (original eight systems re-pinned), and a threefold corpus expansion to verify findings across approximately four million lines of code.
AI.result: The audit yielded 13 cross-cutting observations and a catalog of 29 recurring design patterns. Two significant absences were identified across all systems: no agent runtime imports a general-purpose agentic framework, and none uses vector embeddings for code retrieval. SKILL.md skills outpace MCP in adoption (9/11 vs. 8/11), and ACP (Agent Computer Protocol) ships in six systems with a new third role: harness hosting. The longitudinal sample revealed convergence becoming imitation and behavioral policy migrating from prompt prose to configuration.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that in the first half of 2026, the coding harness completed a turn from tool to platform. This shift represents a fundamental maturation of agent runtimes. The study provides 18 design recommendations and a 90-line minimum-viable-harness scaffold, establishing a foundation for the emerging discipline of harness engineering.

title: A Cone-Constrained Bilinear Decomposition for Total Scaled-Gradient Variation Models
summary: The total scaled-gradient variation (TSGV) regularizer, derived from sparse modeling of piecewise-linear structures, has been shown to preserve edges and corners in image restoration. However, its highly nonconvex and nonlinear nature poses severe computational challenges, as existing methods often suffer from parameter sensitivity or lack convergence guarantees. To overcome this, we propose a tailored bilinear decomposition that decouples the nonlinear weighted gradient in the TSGV regularizer. This approach yields an equivalent optimization problem governed by cone or sphere constraints, depending on the chosen scaling function. In particular, the cone constraint plays a central role in characterizing edge- and corner-preserving behavior. We solve this reformulation using the alternating minimization method (AMM) equipped with a majorization--minimization strategy, ensuring a monotonic decrease in energy without step-size tuning. Furthermore, we provide a geometric interpretation of the edge-preserving properties of these constraints by analyzing their asymptotic behavior near image singularities. We establish the global convergence of the proposed method to a critical point within the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz framework. Extensive numerical experiments on Gaussian denoising and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging show that the proposed method achieves PSNR and SSIM competitive with or superior to representative variational methods, especially at high noise levels, and improves the structural reconstruction under dense and sparse scanning.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses computational challenges in the total scaled-gradient variation (TSGV) regularizer for edge-preserving image restoration. The authors propose a bilinear decomposition that converts the nonconvex problem into one with cone or sphere constraints, solvable via alternating minimization with majorization-minimization. The method achieves competitive or superior results on Gaussian denoising and NLOS imaging, particularly at high noise levels.
AI.motivation: The TSGV regularizer can preserve edges and corners in image restoration but suffers from severe computational challenges due to its highly nonconvex and nonlinear nature. Existing methods face parameter sensitivity or lack convergence guarantees, motivating the need for a more efficient and theoretically grounded approach.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) A tailored bilinear decomposition that decouples the nonlinear weighted gradient in TSGV, reformulating the problem with cone or sphere constraints; (2) An alternating minimization method (AMM) equipped with a majorization-minimization strategy for solving the reformulated problem, ensuring monotonic energy decrease without step-size tuning; (3) Geometric analysis of edge-preserving properties via asymptotic behavior near image singularities.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves PSNR and SSIM competitive with or superior to representative variational methods on Gaussian denoising and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging, especially at high noise levels, and improves structural reconstruction under dense and sparse scanning.
AI.conclusion: The bilinear decomposition with cone constraints provides an effective solution to the TSGV computational challenges. The method guarantees global convergence to a critical point within the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz framework and demonstrates superior performance in edge preservation, particularly under high noise conditions.

title: HyperWorld: Hypergraph-Structured State Serialization Improves Learned Textual World Models
summary: World models enable language-model agents to predict environment dynamics and plan before acting. In text environments, the model must learn symbolic action effects from serialized state descriptions, but the role of serialization structure remains underexplored. We present HyperWorld, a controlled study of state serialization for learned textual world models. We compare raw observations with three symbolic serializations of the same ground-truth state: independent sentences, pairwise triples, and entity-centered hyperedge units that group multiple related facts around entities and relations. All variants use the same training objective: given a state and an action, predict symbolic effects or judge the action infeasible. Across model scales, data budgets, and in-distribution and out-of-distribution test worlds, hyperedge serialization gives the clearest gains for 0.5B--1.5B models and under distribution shift. Larger models reduce the gap, and pairwise triples can match or slightly exceed hyperedges on in-distribution exact match, but hyperedges achieve the strongest out-of-distribution fact F1 and the best small-to-medium scale trade-off between feasibility detection and effect prediction. In downstream greedy planning, the hyperedge world model also attains the highest success rate among the tested representations. These results show that higher-order state organization is a simple but effective inductive bias for learned symbolic world models, especially when model capacity is limited or test environments differ from training.

title: Heard but Not Heeded: Paralinguistic Information Encoding and Loss in Audio-Language Models
summary: Audio language models are designed to understand speech, yet it remains unclear whether they capture how something is said beyond what is said. We present a mechanistic analysis of paralinguistic information in four open source models, Whisper-large-v2, Qwen2-Audio-7B Instruct, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, and Chroma-4B, using the Expresso dataset with controlled speaking styles. We combine centered kernel alignment, linear probing with leave one speaker out evaluation, open ended tone prediction, and a content prosody leakage metric to trace how style information moves from the audio encoder to the final output. All models strongly encode speaking style in the late encoder, that is, the top third of the audio encoder's layers, but this information is consistently degraded before reaching the output. The projector reshapes representation geometry without removing information, while decoders differ in how much style they preserve depending on architecture and training objective. At the output level, models fall into two behaviors. Some are content driven, where predictions depend mainly on text. Others are acoustic driven, where predictions vary with speaking style. The leakage metric quantifies this difference, and qualitative results confirm it. Overall, we identify a gap between what models encode and what they use, highlighting a key limitation in current audio language models.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a gap between what audio language models encode about speaking style (paralinguistic information) and what they actually use in their outputs. While all four models strongly encode speaking style in late encoder layers, this information is consistently degraded before reaching the final output.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear whether audio language models capture "how something is said" beyond "what is said" - i.e., paralinguistic information like speaking style, tone, and prosody. This is important for understanding model capabilities and limitations.
AI.method: The authors analyzed four open-source models (Whisper-large-v2, Qwen2-Audio-7B Instruct, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Chroma-4B) using the Expresso dataset with controlled speaking styles. They combined: (1) centered kernel alignment, (2) linear probing with leave-one-speaker-out evaluation, (3) open-ended tone prediction, and (4) a content prosody leakage metric to trace style information flow from audio encoder to output.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) All models strongly encode speaking style in the late encoder (top third of audio encoder layers), but this information is consistently degraded before reaching output. (2) The projector reshapes representation geometry without removing information. (3) Decoders differ in style preservation depending on architecture and training objective. (4) At output level, models fall into two behaviors: content-driven (predictions depend mainly on text) vs acoustic-driven (predictions vary with speaking style). The leakage metric quantifies this difference.
AI.conclusion: There exists a significant gap between what audio language models encode and what they actually use, highlighting a key limitation in current audio language models regarding paralinguistic information processing.

title: REAL-Q: E2E LLM Quantization via Dynamic Gradient Descent
comment: Proposes a highly efficient end-to-end LLM quantization paradigm that significantly outperforms most existing state-of-the-art baselines
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is essential for deploying large language models (LLMs) under strict resource constraints. State-of-the-art PTQ methods quantize each layer with a single closed-form second-order solver: to remain analytically tractable, they heavily approximate the global loss (dropping cross-channel coupling, pooling output rows into groups), and they then freeze the resulting Hessian across the entire layer, with no way to refresh it as the loss landscape shifts column by column--a phenomenon we call information misalignment. We propose REAL-Q (Real-time E2E-loss Aligned LLM Quantization), a novel PTQ paradigm that breaks this compromise: instead of diluting the objective for the sake of analytic tractability, REAL-Q targets an end-to-end-aligned surrogate of the global loss and refines it via fine-grained, dynamic Block-wise Gradient Descent applied after every column block (128 columns). By coupling this fine-grained correction with a sliding window mechanism for smooth cross-layer transitions, REAL-Q effectively mitigates error propagation across the network. On LLaMA-3.1 (8B and 70B) and Qwen3 (0.6B-32B) at W4A16, REAL-Q reduces end-to-end KL divergence by up to ~49% relative to state-of-the-art globally-guided methods.

AI.tldr: REAL-Q is a novel post-training quantization (PTQ) paradigm for LLMs that uses fine-grained dynamic Block-wise Gradient Descent with a sliding window mechanism to address "information misalignment" in existing methods. It achieves up to 49% reduction in KL divergence compared to state-of-the-art methods on LLaMA-3.1 and Qwen3 models at W4A16 quantization.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art PTQ methods use single closed-form second-order solvers that heavily approximate the global loss (dropping cross-channel coupling, pooling output rows into groups) and freeze the Hessian across the entire layer. This causes "information misalignment" - the loss landscape shifts column by column but the Hessian cannot refresh, leading to suboptimal quantization.
AI.method: REAL-Q targets an end-to-end-aligned surrogate of the global loss and refines it via fine-grained, dynamic Block-wise Gradient Descent applied after every column block (128 columns). It couples this fine-grained correction with a sliding window mechanism for smooth cross-layer transitions to mitigate error propagation.
AI.result: On LLaMA-3.1 (8B and 70B) and Qwen3 (0.6B-32B) at W4A16 quantization, REAL-Q reduces end-to-end KL divergence by up to ~49% relative to state-of-the-art globally-guided methods.
AI.conclusion: REAL-Q effectively breaks the compromise between analytic tractability and quantization accuracy by using dynamic, fine-grained optimization that remains aligned with the end-to-end loss, outperforming existing PTQ methods significantly.

title: Mind the Rift: Cross-Scale Coupling Mismatch for AI-Generated Video Detection
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This version includes the supplementary material as Appendix A-E
summary: As AI video generators achieve cinematic realism, reliable detection becomes essential for safeguarding digital trust. We identify cross-scale coupling mismatch as a new forensic signal, where scale refers to the level of abstraction (semantic dynamics vs. pixel-level residuals): in natural videos, macro-level temporal dynamics and micro-level residual patterns are intrinsically coupled by the unified imaging physics pipeline, whereas AI generators, whose training objectives do not explicitly preserve this joint distribution, systematically violate this coupling. Detecting such mismatch is challenging because it requires independently extracting information at both scales while simultaneously quantifying their cross-scale relationship. We propose RIFT (Representation Inconsistency Forensics on Trajectories), an orthogonal forensic framework that addresses this through three interlocking components: a macro stream that builds a dynamic baseline of expected temporal evolution via differential geometry and persistent homology on learned manifold trajectories, a micro stream that acts as a sensitive forensic probe via steganalytic filtering and temporal modeling, and a coupling divergence module that measures the conditional dependency between the two streams. Gram-Schmidt orthogonality guarantees the information-theoretic validity of this measurement. Experiments on two benchmarks (VidProM, 120K videos, 7 generators; GenVidBench, 68K videos, 4 generators) demonstrate that RIFT achieves 99.33% and 99.72% F1-score respectively, with 97.87% unseen-generator detection rate in leave-one-out evaluation, while exhibiting encoder agnosticism: scaling from ViT-S/14 (22M) to ViT-L/14 (300M) changes F1 by less than 0.1%, and switching to a different encoder family (DINOv1) reduces F1 by only 0.73 pp. Code is available at https://github.com/Litsay/RIFT

AI.tldr: RIFT proposes detecting AI-generated videos by identifying cross-scale coupling mismatch between semantic dynamics (macro-scale) and pixel-level residuals (micro-scale), which are naturally coupled in real videos but broken in AI-generated content. The method uses three components: macro stream (differential geometry/persistent homology), micro stream (steganalytic filtering), and coupling divergence module (Gram-Schmidt orthogonality). Achieves 99%+ F1 on two benchmarks with strong encoderagnosticism.
AI.motivation: As AI video generators achieve cinematic realism, reliable detection becomes essential for safeguarding digital trust. The key insight is that natural videos have intrinsic coupling between macro-level temporal dynamics and micro-level residual patterns due to unified imaging physics, while AI generators systematically violate this coupling since their training objectives don't preserve this joint distribution.
AI.method: RIFT employs three interlocking components: (1) Macro stream - builds dynamic baseline via differential geometry and persistent homology on learned manifold trajectories; (2) Micro stream - acts as forensic probe via steganalytic filtering and temporal modeling; (3) Coupling divergence module - measures conditional dependency between streams using Gram-Schmidt orthogonality to guarantee information-theoretic validity.
AI.result: Experiments on VidProM (120K videos, 7 generators) and GenVidBench (68K videos, 4 generators) show 99.33% and 99.72% F1-score respectively. Leave-one-out evaluation achieves 97.87% unseen-generator detection. Encoderagnosticism: scaling from ViT-S/14 (22M) to ViT-L/14 (300M) changes F1 by <0.1%, switching to DINOv1 reduces F1 by only 0.73pp.
AI.conclusion: RIFT introduces a novel forensic signal (cross-scale coupling mismatch) that is highly effective for AI video detection, achieving state-of-the-art performance with strong generalization to unseen generators and excellent encoderagnosticism, making it practical for real-world deployment.

title: Inverse Rig Optimization from Line Drawings
summary: Stylized 3D character animation is largely hand-authored, with animators authoring rig parameters one keyframe at a time to find the best pose. Because stylized work reads chiefly through contour lines, drawing contours in the camera view is the most direct and precise way to express artistic intent. This mismatch between the rig controls and the artist's goal forces a laborious trial-and-error workflow, with animators repeatedly manipulating rig controls against the rendered view to match the desired contour. To address this, we propose a method that recovers rig parameters from screen-space contour strokes, enabling effective keyframing from sketches. Given strokes that redraw the current contour, our method optimizes the high-level rig parameters defined in the DCC tool. The key is to use a pre-trained MLP rig surrogate that provides a differentiable map from rig parameters to mesh vertices, replacing the original black-box rig within the optimization process. We match user-drawn lines to mesh contour lines and backpropagate the resulting screen-space error through the surrogate to update the rig parameters. Our results demonstrate that the method works for diverse characters and practical scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to recover 3D rig parameters from 2D contour sketches, enabling animators to keyframe stylized characters by drawing desired contours rather than manipulating complex rig controls manually.
AI.motivation: Stylized 3D character animation requires animators to manually adjust rig parameters keyframe-by-keyframe, which is laborious and inefficient because stylized work relies primarily on contour lines, but the rig controls don't directly map to the artist's goal of drawing contours in camera view.
AI.method: The method uses a pre-trained MLP as a differentiable rig surrogate that maps rig parameters to mesh vertices. It matches user-drawn contour strokes to mesh contour lines and backpropagates screen-space error through the surrogate to optimize the rig parameters.
AI.result: The method successfully recovers rig parameters from contour sketches for diverse characters and practical animation scenarios, enabling direct keyframing from sketches.
AI.conclusion: This approach bridges the gap between 2D artistic intent and 3D rig manipulation, significantly streamlining the stylized character animation workflow by allowing artists to draw desired contours rather than trial-and-error manipulation of rig controls.

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence and the Limits of Traditional Systems Theory
summary: This paper examines a foundational assumption in traditional systems theory, namely that structure (the organization of components) and behavior (the evolution of system activity over time) can be treated as separable analytical dimensions. It argues that this separation contributes to persistent difficulties in explaining system identity, particularly in cases involving change, emergence, and boundary specification. To address this issue, the paper introduces Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as a reframing principle. SBC proposes that structure and behavior should not be understood as independently existing entities that are subsequently related through modeling constructs, but as mutually constitutive aspects of a single systemic process. From this perspective, system identity is understood as arising from the sustained co-determination of structural organization and behavioral dynamics, rather than from their external correspondence or alignment. This reframing provides a unified way of understanding system identity, emergence, and boundary formation within a cybernetically informed systems perspective.

title: I-CARE: Analysis of interference-related phenomena in a controllable, diverse and representative unlearning setting for text-to-image models
summary: Machine unlearning studies the removal of knowledge from an AI model, making the system forget a concept it previously learned. Despite rapid progress in generative machine unlearning, the unintended degradation of semantically related concepts that should have been retained (henceforth, interference) remains poorly characterized and inconsistently evaluated. This paper introduces I-CARE, a methodology that formalizes interference as a first-class object of study in generative unlearning. Rather than proposing a new benchmark or unlearning algorithm, I-CARE provides formal definitions for tasks, metrics, and templates for reporting results, enabling the systematic and reproducible study of interference across unlearning settings. While our methodology is designed to remain valid as models and unlearning algorithms evolve, decoupling long-term scientific insight from transient empirical results, we present a feasibility demonstration with state-of-the-art algorithms and frequently used datasets. The results demonstrate that I-CARE enables meaningful analysis of interference patterns across multiple unlearning settings, establishing the practical applicability of the framework. The software implementation of the methodology is provided in an open-source framework, together with a web-based graphical interface that enables exploration of the outcomes of this study without requiring direct interaction with the codebase or specialized data analysis tools.

AI.tldr: I-CARE is a methodology for systematically studying interference (unintended degradation of retained concepts) in generative machine unlearning, providing formal task definitions, metrics, and reporting templates, with open-source implementation and GUI.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning research has rapidly progressed but lacks systematic methods to evaluate interference - the unintended degradation of related concepts that should be retained. Current evaluation is inconsistent and poorly characterized.
AI.method: I-CARE formalizes interference as a first-class study object by providing: (1) formal definitions for tasks, (2) standardized metrics, and (3) reporting templates. Demonstrated with state-of-the-art algorithms on common datasets.
AI.result: I-CARE enables meaningful analysis of interference patterns across multiple unlearning settings, establishing practical applicability. The framework is released as open-source software with a web-based GUI for exploration.
AI.conclusion: I-CARE provides a systematic, reproducible approach to studying interference in generative unlearning that remains valid as models and algorithms evolve, decoupling long-term scientific insight from transient empirical results.

title: Perceptible or Not? Diagnosing Passive Fingerprints for Speech Deepfake Attribution
summary: Passive fingerprints (intrinsic traces naturally left by generators) have been shown to enable attribution in speech deepfake detection, yet their persistence, reproducibility, and content-independence remain unverified. Moreover, no prior work distinguishes perceptible from imperceptible fingerprints, although the two have very different implications for attribution reliability. Perceptible fingerprints, such as emotional expression, are shaped by perceptual quality objectives and may change across model updates, whereas imperceptible fingerprints are not explicitly optimised by current training objectives and are rarely considered in existing dataset design or training strategies, as they have limited influence on downstream applications. We therefore propose a Perceptible-Imperceptible Passive-fingerprint Diagnostic Protocol (PIPDP) to define and separately analyze these two fingerprint types. PIPDP comprises three complementary analyses: multi-evidence fingerprint verification through residual-energy, reproducibility, and saliency analyses, perceptually transparent perturbations preserving audio quality, and prompt-driven emotion change that modifies perceptible fingerprints without model retraining. Experiments across ten speech generators and three attribution detectors show that imperceptible fingerprints provide persistent attribution cues. Perceptually transparent perturbations reduce attribution accuracy by up to 48.2\% on HiggsAudioV3, whereas emotion-driven changes leave attribution largely unchanged, with only about a 1.0\% accuracy variation across emotions on CosyVoice2 using w2v-bert-MLP. These results suggest that imperceptible fingerprints are more reliable for trustworthy attribution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PIPDP, a diagnostic protocol to distinguish perceptible from imperceptible passive fingerprints in speech deepfake detection. The study analyzes 10 speech generators and 3 attribution detectors, finding that imperceptible fingerprints provide more reliable attribution cues than perceptible ones (emotional expressions).
AI.motivation: Current research on passive fingerprints for speech deepfake attribution lacks verification of their persistence, reproducibility, and content-independence. Additionally, no prior work distinguishes between perceptible fingerprints (e.g., emotional expression) that may change across model updates versus imperceptible fingerprints that are not explicitly optimized but may be more reliable for attribution.
AI.method: PIPDP comprises three complementary analyses: (1) multi-evidence fingerprint verification through residual-energy, reproducibility, and saliency analyses; (2) perceptually transparent perturbations preserving audio quality; and (3) prompt-driven emotion change that modifies perceptible fingerprints without model retraining. Experiments were conducted across ten speech generators and three attribution detectors.
AI.result: Perceptually transparent perturbations reduce attribution accuracy by up to 48.2% on HiggsAudioV3, while emotion-driven changes produce only ~1.0% accuracy variation across emotions on CosyVoice2 using w2v-bert-MLP. Imperceptible fingerprints provide persistent attribution cues, whereas perceptible fingerprints (emotional expression) are more susceptible to modification.
AI.conclusion: Imperceptible fingerprints are more reliable than perceptible fingerprints for trustworthy attribution in speech deepfake detection. The findings suggest that future dataset design and training strategies should prioritize imperceptible fingerprints for developing more robust and reliable attribution systems.

title: Convergence issues in Relational Concept Analysis based on AOC-posets
summary: Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) is an approach for conceptual classification building and rule discovery from a binary table describing a set of objects by a set of attributes. Extensions have been proposed to deal with non-binary and more complex data, such as Relational Concept Analysis (RCA) for multi-relational data. RCA aims to highlight groups of objects characterized by their relationships with other groups of objects. The richer and more complex nature of the underlying data allows RCA to produce richer results than FCA, at the expense of higher computational and interpretive complexity. The most commonly used conceptual classification structure in FCA is the concept lattice. However, in many applications, concept lattice substructures, such as AOC-posets, are preferred over the full lattice, either to mitigate combinatorial blow-up or to focus on the most informative parts of the structure. Indeed, in an AOC-poset, only concepts introducing an object or an attribute are represented, which makes AOC-posets smaller and easier to compute and use than concept lattices. Although RCA was originally defined on concept lattices, it can also be instantiated on AOC-posets. RCA is iterative and its convergence is guaranteed in the lattice-based setting, but this guarantee is lost when using AOC-posets. In this paper, we investigate this loss of convergence in detail. We show why convergence is no longer guaranteed in the general case, identify conditions under which it can still be ensured, and discuss how a dataset can be transformed to recover convergence. We also propose a convergent variant of the process, which preserves the AOC-poset structure: relational attributes, once created, are never removed, which guarantees convergence at the price of attributes that may refer to concepts absent from the final structures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why Relational Concept Analysis (RCA) loses its convergence guarantee when applied to AOC-posets instead of full concept lattices. RCA is an extension of Formal Concept Analysis for multi-relational data, and AOC-posets are smaller, more focused substructures of concept lattices. While RCA converges in lattice-based settings, this property fails in AOC-poset-based RCA. The authors identify the conditions under which convergence can be ensured and propose a convergent variant that preserves the AOC-poset structure by never removing newly created relational attributes.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental limitation in RCA when using AOC-posets instead of full concept lattices. In many applications, AOC-posets are preferred over full lattices due to their smaller size and reduced computational complexity. However, the iterative RCA process that converges in lattice-based settings loses this guarantee with AOC-posets. Understanding why convergence is lost and how to recover it is crucial for practical applications of RCA.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze the RCA process when instantiated on AOC-posets. They examine why convergence fails in the general case, identify specific conditions that ensure convergence, and investigate dataset transformations that can recover convergence. They also propose a modified RCA variant that guarantees convergence by preserving relational attributes once created.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate that convergence is no longer guaranteed in the general case when RCA is applied to AOC-posets. They identify specific conditions under which convergence can still be ensured and show how certain dataset transformations can recover convergence. Additionally, they propose a convergent variant that maintains the AOC-poset structure by never removing relational attributes, though this may result in attributes referring to concepts absent from final structures.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a fundamental theoretical limitation of AOC-poset-based RCA and provides practical solutions. Researchers and practitioners can either ensure specific conditions are met to guarantee convergence or use the proposed convergent variant. This work bridges the gap between theoretical foundations and practical applications of RCA in contexts where AOC-posets are preferred over full concept lattices.

title: Jailbreaking Text-to-Image Models Through Cracks: Navigating Heterogeneous Safety Filters via Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content, despite increasingly being guarded by heterogeneous, multi-layer safety stacks combining text filters, image classifiers, and cross-modal detectors. Existing jailbreak studies either optimize against individual filters or query the complete pipeline with aggregate feedback, making it difficult to identify the active constraint and adapt to conflicts across safety layers.In this paper, we introduce the \emph{Detection Surface}, a unified geometric framework that characterizes the decision boundaries induced by heterogeneous T2I safety filters and their joint effect on the jailbreak search space. This formulation reveals that successful evasion is governed by a sparse and non-convex region shaped by cross-layer conflicts, where mutations that bypass one filter may increase exposure to another. Motivated by this analysis, we propose \emph{CRACK}, a multi-agent debate framework for adaptive jailbreak search that decomposes jailbreak search into exploration, diagnosis, and arbitration. CRACK coordinates an Attack Agent, a Defense Agent, and a Judge Agent to iteratively generate prompt mutations, obtain layer-specific diagnostic feedback, and optimize mutation strategies through reward-guided refinement. Through repeated rounds of debate, CRACK adapts its search direction to the evolving cross-layer constraints while preserving the original harmful intent. Extensive experiments across multiple T2I models, datasets, and safety configurations show that CRACK achieves Attack Success Rates (ASR) of up to 99.63\% under composite defenses, while requiring fewer queries than existing methods and maintaining semantic fidelity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Detection Surface, a geometric framework for analyzing jailbreak attacks against heterogeneous T2I safety filters, and proposes CRACK, a multi-agent debate system that achieves up to 99.63% attack success rate by adapting to cross-layer constraints across text filters, image classifiers, and cross-modal detectors.
AI.motivation: Current jailbreak research fails to identify which specific safety filter is being triggered or how to handle conflicts between multiple defensive layers. Existing approaches either optimize against single filters or test the complete pipeline without diagnostic feedback, making it difficult to understand and adapt to composite defenses.
AI.method: The paper proposes two contributions: (1) Detection Surface - a geometric framework modeling decision boundaries of heterogeneous safety filters and their joint effect on the jailbreak search space, revealing sparse non-convex evasion regions shaped by cross-layer conflicts; (2) CRACK - a multi-agent debate framework with three agents (Attack, Defense, Judge) that iteratively generates prompt mutations, obtains layer-specific diagnostic feedback, and optimizes strategies through reward-guided refinement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple T2I models, datasets, and safety configurations demonstrate that CRACK achieves Attack Success Rates (ASR) of up to 99.63% under composite defenses, requires fewer queries than existing methods, and maintains semantic fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The Detection Surface framework reveals that successful evasion depends on sparse, non-convex regions shaped by conflicts between safety layers. CRACK's multi-agent debate approach effectively adapts to evolving cross-layer constraints, representing a significant advancement in understanding and evaluating T2I safety systems.

title: HyperSketch: Controllable Video Sketching in a Style Hyperspace
summary: Vector sketch animation offers tremendous advantages for multimedia and creative design through concise line expressions and flexible editing. Learning-based generation methods of sketch animation have made significant progress in the last decade, but still suffer from limited style diversity and controllability. This paper presents a controllable video sketching method that automatically converts videos into multi-style vector sketch animations. A continuous style hyperspace is constructed by multi-dimensional sketch styles (fidelity, simplicity, text guidance strength) and the timeline. With this hyperspace, stroke control points are parameterized as 4-variable Bernstein polynomials, ensuring smooth and differentiable style transitions. A multi-task, multi-stage optimization framework is designed to learn stroke hyperparameters accurately and efficiently. We further developed a web-based interactive interface that allows real-time style manipulation via editable curves. Experiments show the style controllability, high-quality, and user-friendliness of our method, which outperforms SOTA methods.

AI.tldr: A controllable video-to-sketch animation method that converts videos into multi-style vector sketch animations using a continuous style hyperspace parameterized byBernstein polynomials, with an interactive web interface for real-time style manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based sketch animation generation methods suffer from limited style diversity and controllability, necessitating a more flexible and controllable approach for multimedia and creative design applications.
AI.method: 1) Construct a continuous style hyperspace with multi-dimensional sketch styles (fidelity, simplicity, text guidance strength) and timeline; 2) Parameterize stroke control points as 4-variable Bernstein polynomials for smooth/differentiable style transitions; 3) Design a multi-task, multi-stage optimization framework for learning stroke hyperparameters; 4) Develop a web-based interactive interface with editable curves for real-time style manipulation.
AI.result: The method demonstrates style controllability, high-quality output, and user-friendliness, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed controllable video sketching method successfully enables automatic conversion of videos into multi-style vector sketch animations with smooth style transitions and intuitive user control, advancing the field of vector sketch animation generation.

title: What Is a System? An Interaction-Based Account of Structure-Behavior Coalescence in General Systems Theory
summary: The question of what constitutes a system remains fundamental to General Systems Theory. Existing definitions commonly characterize a system in terms of elements, relationships, boundaries, functions, or interactions, but these perspectives do not always provide a unified account of how system structure and system behavior constitute one another. This paper proposes Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as an interaction-based account of what a system is. From the SBC perspective, a system is not merely a collection of elements or relationships, nor is it adequately characterized by behavior considered independently of structure. Rather, a system is a structured entity whose behavior arises through interactions among its constituent entities, with those interactions simultaneously contributing to both its structural organization and behavioral realization. The paper develops this perspective by distinguishing system structure, interaction, and behavior while treating them as inseparable aspects of a unified system representation. It argues that interactions provide the essential link through which structural relationships become behavioral processes and through which behavioral processes reveal and instantiate system structure. This perspective provides a basis for representing systems in a manner that maintains consistency between what a system is and what a system does. The paper further considers the implications of SBC for General Systems Theory, particularly for system identity, system boundaries, behavioral emergence, and the representation of complex systems. SBC is presented as a general conceptual foundation that complements existing systems theories by placing the coalescence of structure and behavior through interaction at the center of the definition of a system.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as a new conceptual framework for understanding what constitutes a system in General Systems Theory. SBC addresses the limitation that existing definitions treat system structure and behavior as separate entities, when in fact they are inseparable - interactions simultaneously constitute both structural organization and behavioral realization. This perspective provides a unified account that maintains consistency between what a system is (structure) and what it does (behavior).
AI.motivation: The fundamental question of what constitutes a system remains unresolved in General Systems Theory. Existing definitions characterize systems in terms of elements, relationships, boundaries, functions, or interactions, but these perspectives fail to provide a unified account of how system structure and system behavior constitute one another. The paper seeks to bridge this conceptual gap.
AI.method: The paper develops the SBC perspective by: (1) distinguishing system structure, interaction, and behavior as concepts, (2) treating them as inseparable aspects of a unified system representation, (3) positioning interactions as the essential link through which structural relationships become behavioral processes and vice versa.
AI.result: The SBC perspective provides a basis for representing systems that maintains consistency between what a system is and what a system does. It offers a general conceptual foundation that complements existing systems theories by placing the coalescence of structure and behavior through interaction at the center of the definition of a system.
AI.conclusion: SBC presents a general conceptual foundation that complements existing systems theories. It has implications for understanding system identity, system boundaries, behavioral emergence, and the representation of complex systems. The key insight is that interactions are not merely connections between structure and behavior, but rather the mechanism through which they mutually constitute each other.

title: ZimaBlue: Evolving Generalizable World Action Models through Scalable Video Pre-training
summary: Robotic manipulation faces a fundamental scaling challenge: robust generalization demands broad physical experience, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are expensive to collect and inherently limited in diversity. Egocentric videos offer a far more scalable source of embodied experience, capturing object interactions, contact dynamics, tool use, and long-horizon behaviors across diverse environments. The central challenge is how to convert this abundant but action-free experience into effective robot control. We introduce ZimaBlue, a scalable framework for learning generalizable World Action Models (WAMs) from large-scale video. ZimaBlue follows a three-stage training curriculum: it first performs causal embodied video pre-training on large-scale human and robot egocentric videos, then grounds the learned visual dynamics in heterogeneous robot trajectories through video-action mid-training with a unified action representation, and finally specializes the model to a target robot for deployment. To make generative WAMs practical for real-time control, ZimaBluefurther adopts an asynchronous Slow-Fast dual-system architecture, where a high-capacity Slow world model provides generalizable spatiotemporal representations and a lightweight Fast branch enables 30 Hz action prediction on NVIDIA RTX 4090. On real-robot zero-shot evaluations, scaling from target-robot data alone to over 120,000 hours of embodied video improves success from 36.1% to 77.8%. ZimaBlue further delivers strong performance across multiple benchmarks, with particularly pronounced gains on unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: ZimaBlue is a scalable framework for learning generalizable World Action Models (WAMs) from large-scale egocentric video data for robotic manipulation. It uses a three-stage training curriculum (pre-training, mid-training, specialization) and a Slow-Fast dual-system architecture for real-time control. The approach achieves significant improvements in zero-shot generalization, increasing success rates from 36.1% to 77.8% when scaling from target-robot data alone to over 120,000 hours of embodied video.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation faces a fundamental scaling challenge: robust generalization requires broad physical experience, but action-labeled robot trajectories are expensive to collect and limited in diversity. Egocentric videos offer a more scalable source of embodied experience, but the central challenge is converting this abundant but action-free experience into effective robot control.
AI.method: ZimaBlue employs a three-stage training curriculum: (1) Causal embodied video pre-training on large-scale human and robot egocentric videos; (2) Video-action mid-training with a unified action representation to ground learned visual dynamics in heterogeneous robot trajectories; (3) Specialization to target robot for deployment. It also uses an asynchronous Slow-Fast dual-system architecture with a high-capacity Slow world model for generalizable representations and a lightweight Fast branch enabling 30 Hz action prediction.
AI.result: Scaling from target-robot data alone to over 120,000 hours of embodied video improves zero-shot success from 36.1% to 77.8%. The method delivers strong performance across multiple benchmarks, with particularly pronounced gains on unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: ZimaBlue successfully bridges the gap between action-free egocentric video data and effective robot control through a scalable curriculum learning approach and efficient dual-system architecture, demonstrating that large-scale video pre-training can significantly improve robotic manipulation generalization.

title: Discrete-Time MDP Modeling for Multi-Item Capacitated Lot Sizing with Stochastic Demand Timing
summary: This paper studies a finite-horizon multi-item capacitated lot-sizing problem in which demand quantities are deterministic, while demand-arrival periods are stochastic. Each demand occurs once within a known time window and must be satisfied no later than its deadline. The proposed model makes production and allocation decisions at the demand level, allowing it to represent capacity competition, demand-specific backlog, and allocation-dependent inventory dynamics. The stochastic problem is formulated as a discrete-time Markov decision process (DTMDP), including the state space, feasible actions, transition kernel, and one-period cost function. To isolate the computational effect of stochastic timing, each stochastic instance is first compared with a deterministic counterpart in which each arrival distribution is replaced by its most likely arrival period. This comparison shows that stochastic timing substantially increases the number of states, the number of transitions, solution time, and memory pressure. A genetic algorithm (GA) is then proposed for the stochastic-timing problem. The GA searches over feasible state-feedback policies and evaluates each policy exactly under the DTMDP transition model. Computational experiments on 330 benchmark instances show that the GA remains close to the exact stochastic solution whenever the latter is available, with an average optimality gap of about $3.44\%$. On the difficult benchmark instances, comprising 90 test cases, the GA remains below the $5\%$ optimality-gap threshold and achieves an average optimization speedup of $6.89 \pm 1.41$ at the $95\%$ confidence level. For instances that cannot be solved exactly on the available hardware, an empirical Bellman-time regression is used to estimate the missing exact resolution time and extrapolate the expected GA speedup.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a finite-horizon multi-item capacitated lot-sizing problem with stochastic demand-arrival periods but deterministic quantities. Demand must be satisfied by deadlines. The problem is formulated as a Discrete-Time Markov Decision Process (DTMDP). A genetic algorithm (GA) is developed to find near-optimal solutions, achieving an average optimality gap of 3.44% and speedups of 6.89±1.41 on difficult instances.
AI.motivation: The study aims to understand how stochastic timing of demand arrivals affects computational complexity and solution quality in lot-sizing problems. The motivation is to isolate and quantify the computational impact of stochastic timing compared to deterministic counterparts, and to develop an efficient heuristic method for solving these complex problems.
AI.method: 1) Formulated the problem as a DTMDP with state space, feasible actions, transition kernel, and one-period cost function. 2) Compared stochastic instances with deterministic counterparts (using most likely arrival periods) to measure computational impact. 3) Developed a genetic algorithm (GA) that searches over feasible state-feedback policies and evaluates each policy exactly under the DTMDP transition model. 4) Used empirical Bellman-time regression to estimate resolution time for unsolvable instances.
AI.result: Stochastic timing substantially increases computational complexity (states, transitions, solution time, and memory). On 330 benchmark instances, the GA achieved an average optimality gap of ~3.44% compared to exact solutions. On 90 difficult instances, the GA remained below 5% optimality gap with an average speedup of 6.89 ± 1.41 at 95% confidence level.
AI.conclusion: The genetic algorithm effectively handles the stochastic-timing lot-sizing problem, providing near-optimal solutions with significant computational speedups. The study demonstrates that stochastic timing significantly increases problem complexity, and the proposed GA offers a practical approach for instances that cannot be solved exactly with available hardware.

title: MADS: A Multiview Acoustic Descriptor Set Beyond Standard Spectral Summaries
summary: Dominant audio classification pipelines rely either on compact handcrafted summaries or on fixed time-frequency frontends such as log-mel representations prior to deep modeling. While highly successful, these representations do not explicitly expose the physical dynamics of the underlying sound-generating event. We introduce MADS (Multi-view Acoustic Descriptor Set), a compact 19-dimensional physics-informed descriptor set de- signed to capture complementary spectral, temporal, mechanical, and stochastic structure in audio signals. Rather than treating sound only as a spectral pattern, MADS encodes properties related to excitation, damping, periodicity, impulsiveness, and structural consistency within a unified multi-view representation. We evaluate MADS using standard classical machine learning models on ESC-10, ESC-50, and MSoS, and compare it against two conventional handcrafted baselines: a compact 26D MFCC- based baseline and an expanded 38D spectral-summary baseline. Across ESC-10 and ESC-50, MADS achieves the strongest peak results overall, reaching 81.00% and 52.78%, respectively, while using roughly half the dimensionality of the 38D baseline. On MSoS, MADS again delivers the strongest top-end performance, reaching 67.48%. These results establish MADS not merely as a competitive standalone descriptor set, but as the foundational descriptor layer of a broader acoustically grounded representation program for future frame-level and deep-learning-compatible audio modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MADS (Multi-view Acoustic Descriptor Set), a 19-dimensional physics-informed audio descriptor set that captures spectral, temporal, mechanical, and stochastic structure in audio signals. It encodes properties related to excitation, damping, periodicity, impulsiveness, and structural consistency. MADS outperforms conventional MFCC-based baselines on ESC-10, ESC-50, and MSoS datasets while using fewer dimensions.
AI.motivation: Current dominant audio classification pipelines rely on either compact handcrafted summaries or fixed time-frequency frontends (like log-mel representations), but these representations do not explicitly expose the physical dynamics of the underlying sound-generating event. The authors aim to create a physics-informed representation that captures the physical properties of sound generation.
AI.method: The authors designed MADS, a 19-dimensional physics-informed descriptor set that captures complementary spectral, temporal, mechanical, and stochastic structure in audio signals. It encodes properties related to excitation, damping, periodicity, impulsiveness, and structural consistency within a unified multi-view representation. They evaluated MADS using standard classical machine learning models on three datasets (ESC-10, ESC-50, and MSoS) and compared it against two baselines: a compact 26D MFCC-based baseline and an expanded 38D spectral-summary baseline.
AI.result: Across ESC-10 and ESC-50, MADS achieves the strongest peak results overall, reaching 81.00% and 52.78% respectively, while using roughly half the dimensionality of the 38D baseline. On MSoS, MADS again delivers the strongest top-end performance, reaching 67.48%.
AI.conclusion: MADS establishes itself not merely as a competitive standalone descriptor set, but as the foundational descriptor layer of a broader acoustically grounded representation program for future frame-level and deep-learning-compatible audio modeling.

title: DISTAL: Distillation and Self-Supervised Pretraining for Structure-Agnostic Materials Property Prediction
summary: Materials property prediction remains difficult in low-data settings, where many target properties are supported by only a limited number of labeled samples. Models with the strongest predictive accuracy often depend on crystal structures, which restricts their use in early-stage screening when structural information is limited or unavailable. To address this challenge, we propose DISTAL, a dual-prior framework for structure-agnostic materials property prediction that combines self-supervised compositional pretraining with structure-aware knowledge distillation. DISTAL first learns transferable compositional representations from a large virtual composition space using 145 composition-derived descriptors. It then distills structural knowledge from a pretrained ALIGNN teacher into a composition-conditioned student. This setting allows structural priors to be used during training without requiring structural inputs at inference. By integrating explicit compositional descriptors, pretrained latent features, and distilled structural features within a unified prediction pipeline, DISTAL captures complementary signals that are difficult to recover from any single representation alone. Across 39 benchmark tasks, the best-performing multimodal configuration combines all three signals, and improves over the reference benchmark on 37 tasks. DISTAL achieves the strongest overall performance among all evaluated feature combinations. These results indicate that compositional pretraining and structural distillation provide complementary priors and offer a practical route to robust composition-only prediction in small-data materials informatics. The source code and the pre-trained models are anonymously available at: https://osf.io/eq96d/overview?view_only=451617f42f7849e08750bd1852b48980 and will be released at the official link after acceptance.

AI.tldr: DISTAL is a dual-prior framework for structure-agnostic materials property prediction in low-data settings. It combines self-supervised compositional pretraining with structure-aware knowledge distillation to predict materials properties without requiring crystal structures at inference time.
AI.motivation: Materials property prediction is difficult in low-data settings where labeled samples are limited. State-of-the-art models require crystal structures, but structural information is often unavailable during early-stage materials screening.
AI.method: DISTAL combines three components: (1) Self-supervised compositional pretraining using 145 composition-derived descriptors to learn transferable representations from a large virtual composition space; (2) Structure-aware knowledge distillation that transfers knowledge from a pretrained ALIGNN teacher into a composition-conditioned student; (3) A unified prediction pipeline integrating explicit compositional descriptors, pretrained latent features, and distilled structural features.
AI.result: Across 39 benchmark tasks, the best multimodal configuration combining all three signals improves over the reference benchmark on 37 tasks and achieves the strongest overall performance among all evaluated feature combinations.
AI.conclusion: Compositional pretraining and structural distillation provide complementary priors, offering a practical route to robust composition-only prediction in small-data materials informatics.

title: TimeSteer: Inference-Time Speech Scheduling in Joint Audio-Visual Diffusion Models
summary: Although pretrained joint audio-visual diffusion models offer rich control over \emph{what} to generate, they provide no explicit control over \emph{when} an utterance should occur. To address this, we study \emph{inference-time speech scheduling}, a novel task that places coupled speech and visual articulation within user-specified begin--end intervals without finetuning the backbone model.
