title: ReDeck: Step-Level Render-Grounded Refinement for Document-to-Slide Generation
summary: Document-to-slide generation is challenging because slides are dense editable artifacts that require both faithful content selection and precise spatial layout. Recent slide agents adopt iterative reflection, but typically follow a monolithic "one version, one feedback" loop: a slide or deck is rewritten, rendered afterward, and critiqued only at the turn boundary. This delayed feedback makes local failures such as overflow, overlap, clipping, and off-canvas placement difficult to attribute and repair. We propose ReDeck, a step-level render-grounded refinement framework that decomposes slide revision into atomic edit actions and returns renderer-derived observations after each step, turning refinement into "one edit, one observation." To balance local repair with global quality, ReDeck uses multi-granular feedback: step-level render feedback for spatial errors, a turn-level adaptive critic for semantic and design guidance, and a submission-level gate for hard layout validation. We further introduce DeckQuiz, a benchmark that decouples content fidelity, spatial correctness, and design quality. Across GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6, and Gemini-3.1, ReDeck consistently outperforms existing slide-generation agents, and ablations confirm that feedback timing and granularity are critical for reliable slide refinement.

AI.tldr: ReDeck proposes a step-level render-grounded refinement framework for document-to-slide generation that addresses delayed feedback problems in existing slide agents by decomposing revisions into atomic edit actions with renderer-derived observations after each step, using multi-granular feedback at step, turn, and submission levels.
AI.motivation: Current slide generation agents use monolithic 'one version, one feedback' loops where slides are rewritten, rendered, and critiqued only at turn boundaries. This delayed feedback makes local failures (overflow, overlap, clipping, off-canvas placement) difficult to attribute and repair.
AI.method: ReDeck decomposes slide revision into atomic edit actions and returns renderer-derived observations after each step, creating a 'one edit, one observation' refinement loop. It uses multi-granular feedback: (1) step-level render feedback for spatial errors, (2) turn-level adaptive critic for semantic and design guidance, and (3) submission-level gate for hard layout validation. The paper also introduces DeckQuiz benchmark.
AI.result: ReDeck consistently outperforms existing slide-generation agents across GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6, and Gemini-3.1. Ablations confirm that feedback timing and granularity are critical for reliable slide refinement.
AI.conclusion: Step-level render-grounded feedback with multi-granular feedback mechanisms significantly improves slide generation quality. The approach successfully addresses the attribution and repair challenges of local spatial failures in document-to-slide generation.

title: Geometry-aware Latent Autoregressive Generative Model for PDEs in Complex Domains
summary: Solving multiphysics partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a major challenge in scientific computing, especially for highly complex $μ$m-scale tortuous geometries critical to energy and chemical engineering. We address this challenge by proposing a Geometry-aware Latent Autoregressive generative Model for PDEs (GeoLAMP) for solving physics within highly irregular and tortuous structures. GeoLAMP introduces a dual-encoder architecture on graph representations to jointly capture global topology and fine-scale geometric features, enabling an effective transition from real-space fields to compact latent representations. In the latent space, we propose a causal self-attention transformer with flow matching to model temporal dynamics, allowing stable and scalable block-wise autoregressive prediction. A flexible decoder reconstructs high-resolution physical fields on arbitrary points. We establish three multiphysics benchmark datasets in complex geometries, covering reactive flow, heat convection, and elasticity. GeoLAMP consistently achieves the most stable autoregression performance on these datasets, maintaining low errors throughout the entire rollout horizon. Our results provide a systematic study of geometry-aware learning for PDEs in $μ$m-scale complex geometries and offer new insights into block-wise time marching of latent autoregressive PDE modeling via a flow matching framework.

AI.tldr: GeoLAMP is a geometry-aware latent autoregressive deep learning model for solving multiphysics partial differential equations in complex micro-scale tortuous geometries. It uses a dual-encoder graph architecture to capture geometry, a causal transformer with flow matching for temporal modeling, and achieves stable block-wise autoregressive prediction across reactive flow, heat convection, and elasticity benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Solving multiphysics PDEs in highly irregular and tortuous μm-scale geometries remains a major challenge in scientific computing, particularly for energy and chemical engineering applications. Existing methods struggle with complex geometries and long-horizon stability.
AI.method: GeoLAMP introduces: (1) Dual-encoder architecture on graph representations to jointly capture global topology and fine-scale geometric features, enabling transition from real-space to compact latent representations; (2) Causal self-attention transformer with flow matching in latent space to model temporal dynamics; (3) Flexible decoder for high-resolution field reconstruction on arbitrary points. Uses block-wise autoregressive prediction for stable temporal evolution.
AI.result: Three multiphysics benchmark datasets were established covering reactive flow, heat convection, and elasticity in complex geometries. GeoLAMP consistently achieves the most stable autoregression performance, maintaining low errors throughout the entire rollout horizon compared to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: GeoLAMP provides a systematic framework for geometry-aware learning of PDEs in μm-scale complex structures. The combination of dual-encoder graph representations, causal transformer with flow matching, and block-wise autoregressive prediction enables stable and accurate long-horizon predictions, offering new insights into latent autoregressive PDE modeling for multiphysics problems in tortuous geometries.

title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models to Classify Pull Request-Issue Alignments: Going Beyond Prompting
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to Springer Empirical Software Engineering (EMSE), Special Issue on Software Analysis, Evolution, and Reengineering (SANER 2025)
summary:
Context: Accurate alignment between pull requests (PRs) and corresponding issues is crucial for efficient software development and maintaining code quality, as misalignments can reduce traceability, hinder defect localization, and decrease maintainability.
  Objective: This study aims to improve automated PR-issue alignment classification by leveraging fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) across multiple alignment categories, and conducts interpretability analysis to investigate the effects of PR-issue fields on the predictions of fine-tuned LLMs.
  Method: Our methodology consists of dataset preparation, LLM fine-tuning, and interpretability analysis. We first extended an existing dataset and applied data augmentation to address class imbalance. GPT-4o was then fine-tuned via instruction tuning, and open-source LLMs including CodeLlama-7B, CodeQwen1.5-7B, StableCode-3B, CodeGemma-7B, and Deepseek-Coder-6.7B were fine-tuned using classification-specific heads. Interpretability analysis provides actionable insights into the dataset features driving alignment decisions, deepening understanding of how LLMs reason over software artifacts.

title: ViTAL-X: Video-Text Alignment with Cross-Modal Temporal Edits
summary: Video-text models adapted from image-text architectures (e.g., CLIP) frequently exhibit temporal blindness, the inability to perceive fundamental cues like order, direction, and motion dynamics. Standard datasets mask this limitation by enabling models to exploit static spatial shortcuts. To systematically evaluate this, we introduce XTE-Bench, a diagnostic probe revealing that even large-scale video-language models struggle with basic temporal reasoning, indicating that parameter scaling alone is insufficient to resolve this flaw. To address this, we propose Cross-Modal Temporal Edits (XTE), a self-supervised framework that injects precise temporal supervision. By performing synchronized video-text transformations, XTE generates hard temporal negatives without manual annotation. We instantiate this with ViTAL-X, a lightweight model that equips frozen image-text backbones with temporal awareness while preserving their foundational spatial knowledge. Across six temporal benchmarks, ViTAL-X achieves state-of-the-art performance. Utilizing only 0.4B parameters and 1M training clips, ViTAL-X outperforms 7B-parameter models and surpasses baselines trained on 600x more data. These results demonstrate that targeted, high-quality temporal alignment provides a highly efficient alternative to pure scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses temporal blindness in video-text models adapted from image-text architectures (like CLIP), which struggle to perceive order, direction, and motion dynamics. The authors introduce XTE-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark revealing that parameter scaling alone cannot fix this limitation. They propose Cross-Modal Temporal Edits (XTE), a self-supervised framework generating hard temporal negatives via synchronized video-text transformations. ViTAL-X, a lightweight model (0.4B parameters, 1M training clips), achieves SOTA on six temporal benchmarks, outperforming 7B-parameter models and models trained on 600x more data.
AI.motivation: Video-text models adapted from image-text architectures (e.g., CLIP) exhibit temporal blindness - inability to perceive fundamental cues like order, direction, and motion dynamics. Standard datasets mask this limitation by enabling models to exploit static spatial shortcuts. Even large-scale video-language models struggle with basic temporal reasoning, and parameter scaling alone is insufficient to resolve this flaw.
AI.method: 1) XTE-Bench: A diagnostic probe to systematically evaluate temporal reasoning capabilities. 2) Cross-Modal Temporal Edits (XTE): A self-supervised framework that generates hard temporal negatives without manual annotation by performing synchronized video-text transformations. 3) ViTAL-X: A lightweight model that equips frozen image-text backbones with temporal awareness while preserving foundational spatial knowledge.
AI.result: ViTAL-X achieves state-of-the-art performance across six temporal benchmarks. Using only 0.4B parameters and 1M training clips, it outperforms 7B-parameter models and surpasses baselines trained on 600x more data (600x more training data).
AI.conclusion: Targeted, high-quality temporal alignment provides a highly efficient alternative to pure scaling. The work demonstrates that self-supervised temporal supervision through XTE can effectively inject temporal awareness into frozen image-text backbones with minimal computational resources.

title: AI Should Not Only Be Helpful. It Should Be Contingent. Artificial Intimacy, Sycophancy, and the Future of Social Learning
summary:
Conversational artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in everyday social environments, where it functions as both an informational tool and a source of interpersonal feedback. This perspective introduces contingency, i.e., the degree to which system responses vary with user behavior and its interpersonal consequences, as a central construct for evaluating AI systems. We argue that current alignment approaches, including reinforcement learning from human feedback, tend to prioritize user approval and conversational fluency over behaviorally informative feedback, leading to sycophantic patterns of noncontingent affirmation.
  Drawing on behavioral science and social learning theory, we propose that contingent feedback is a key mechanism through which individuals develop interpersonal skills. When AI systems provide feedback weakly coupled to social consequences, they may reduce opportunities for adaptive calibration in real-world interactions, particularly during adolescence, a critical period for social development.
  We outline a framework for contingent AI, including trajectory-based evaluation and models of social consequence prediction, and propose a research agenda spanning developmental psychology, human-AI interaction, and machine learning. More broadly, we argue that AI systems should be evaluated not only by user satisfaction, but by their impact on human social learning.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper argues that current conversational AI systems, optimized for user approval through alignment approaches like RLHF, provide non-contingent feedback that may hinder human social learning, particularly during adolescence. The authors propose a new framework for 'contingent AI' that evaluates systems based on their impact on adaptive social skill development.
AI.motivation: The authors identify a critical gap in how AI systems are evaluated: current approaches prioritize user satisfaction and conversational fluency, but this leads to sycophantic AI behavior that fails to provide behaviorally informative feedback. This is particularly concerning as AI becomes embedded in everyday social environments where it functions as a source of interpersonal feedback.
AI.method: The paper takes a theoretical perspective, drawing on behavioral science and social learning theory to analyze the role of AI in human social development. It proposes a new construct - 'contingency' - as a central evaluation criterion and outlines a framework for contingent AI including trajectory-based evaluation and models of social consequence prediction.
AI.result: The paper establishes contingency (degree to which system responses vary with user behavior and its interpersonal consequences) as a key construct for evaluating AI systems. It identifies the problem of non-contingent affirmation in current AI systems and proposes that contingent feedback is essential for developing interpersonal skills through social learning.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue for a fundamental shift in AI evaluation criteria: systems should be assessed not only by user satisfaction but by their impact on human social learning. They outline a cross-disciplinary research agenda spanning developmental psychology, human-AI interaction, and machine learning to develop and evaluate contingent AI systems that support adaptive social development.

title: Do LLMs Know Your Neighborhood? Auditing LLM Priors for Neighborhood-Level Mobility Prediction and Structural Alignment
summary: Human mobility is central to urban planning, transportation, public health, and emergency response, yet fine-grained trajectory data are often proprietary, restricted, and privacy-sensitive. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential alternative by generating plausible mobility traces and predicting individual movement, but their ability to infer aggregate neighborhood-level mobility remains unclear. We evaluate zero-shot LLMs on Census Block Group-level mobility prediction across four U.S. metropolitan areas using anonymized Cuebiq data to construct point-level, trajectory-level, and temporal mobility outcomes, paired with sociodemographic and built-environment predictors. We compare LLM predictions with supervised baselines and introduce a directional alignment analysis to test whether LLM-implied predictor effects agree with empirical OLS and Jonckheere-Terpstra trends. Supervised models achieve 0.580 average accuracy, compared with 0.435 for the best LLM, with spatial extent outcomes showing the strongest predictability but also the largest LLM-baseline gaps. Directional analysis shows that LLMs often rely on coarse, stable predictor-level priors that remain similar across outcomes and cities, including asymmetric treatment of protected-group predictors. Overall, LLMs can partially recover aggregate mobility patterns from urban context, but their predictions should not be treated as structurally grounded without auditing empirical alignment and potential bias.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates zero-shot LLMs' ability to predict aggregate neighborhood-level mobility across four U.S. metropolitan areas, finding supervised models (0.580 accuracy) significantly outperform LLMs (0.435). LLMs rely on coarse, stable priors rather than structurally grounded predictions.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained trajectory data are proprietary and privacy-sensitive, while LLMs offer a potential alternative for generating mobility traces and predicting individual movement. This study investigates whether LLMs can infer aggregate neighborhood-level mobility patterns.
AI.method: The study uses anonymized Cuebiq data to construct point-level, trajectory-level, and temporal mobility outcomes at the Census Block Group level across four U.S. metropolitan areas. LLMs are evaluated in zero-shot mode and compared with supervised baselines. A directional alignment analysis tests whether LLM-implied predictor effects agree with empirical OLS and Jonckheere-Terpstra trends.
AI.result: Supervised models achieve 0.580 average accuracy versus 0.435 for the best LLM. Spatial extent outcomes show strongest predictability but also largest LLM-baseline gaps. Directional analysis reveals LLMs rely on coarse, stable predictor-level priors across outcomes and cities, including asymmetric treatment of protected-group predictors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can partially recover aggregate mobility patterns from urban context, but their predictions should not be treated as structurally grounded without auditing empirical alignment and potential bias.

title: Reliable LLM-Generated Programs for High-Energy Physics Experiments through Graph-Grounded Software Knowledge
summary: Extracting physics information from modern particle-physics experiments requires multistage analyses implemented on top of large and highly interconnected software ecosystems. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) often produce unreliable programs for such tasks because a user request alone rarely specifies the required APIs, dependencies, and usage conventions. We organize these software relations before generation and retrieve task-relevant knowledge at inference time. Using the open-source ROOT framework as a representative and reproducible testbed, we evaluate a complete grounding system that combines hybrid retrieval over a heterogeneous software knowledge graph, skill-selected workflow examples, and execution-guided repair. On a benchmark of 275 ROOT tasks, grounding improves first-attempt execution from 58.5% to 76.0% under Claude Code orchestration and from 51.3% to 64.0% under standalone orchestration. Final success increases from 90.5% to 96.0% and from 78.9% to 90.9%, respectively, while the average generation cost per successful task increases by only 1.3% and 3.2%. The gains persist under a strong coding agent, indicating that explicit software knowledge remains valuable even when agentic scaffolding is already in place. Because the method captures software relations common to large codebases rather than facts specific to ROOT or a particular model, it should transfer to other experiment frameworks and proprietary software, especially where documentation is sparse or internal dependencies are complex.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a grounding system that improves LLM code generation for particle physics software (ROOT framework) by organizing software relations before generation and retrieving task-relevant knowledge at inference time. The system combines hybrid retrieval over a heterogeneous software knowledge graph, skill-selected workflow examples, and execution-guided repair, significantly improving execution success rates with minimal cost increase.
AI.motivation: Modern particle physics experiments require multistage analyses on large software ecosystems, but general-purpose LLMs produce unreliable programs because user requests alone rarely specify required APIs, dependencies, and usage conventions.
AI.method: The authors developed a complete grounding system that: (1) organizes software relations before generation, (2) retrieves task-relevant knowledge at inference time using hybrid retrieval over a heterogeneous software knowledge graph, (3) uses skill-selected workflow examples, and (4) implements execution-guided repair. Evaluated on 275 ROOT tasks under both Claude Code orchestration and standalone orchestration.
AI.result: Grounding improved first-attempt execution from 58.5% to 76.0% (Claude) and from 51.3% to 64.0% (standalone). Final success increased from 90.5% to 96.0% (Claude) and from 78.9% to 90.9% (standalone), while average generation cost per successful task increased by only 1.3% and 3.2%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit software knowledge remains valuable even with agentic scaffolding in place. The method captures software relations common to large codebases rather than framework-specific facts, suggesting transferability to other experiment frameworks and proprietary software, especially where documentation is sparse or internal dependencies are complex.

title: Soft-Argmax for the Projective Plane via the Veronese Embedding
summary: From horizon detection to fibre structures in X-ray imaging, many vision tasks recover lines via peak detection in Hough space $H=S^1\times\mathbb{R}$, the domain of orientation-offset pairs $(θ,ρ)$. Differentiable pipelines extract coordinates via \emph{soft-argmax}, a probability-weighted average that is only meaningful in a globally linear space. However, $(θ,ρ)$ and $(θ+π,-ρ)$ describe the same undirected line, so $H$ double-covers the space of undirected lines $H/\mathbb{Z}_2$: a Möbius strip, obtained by identifying each pair under $\mathbb{Z}_2$ action. Soft-argmax operates on the cover $H$, but since $H/\mathbb{Z}_2$ admits no linear structure, it tears geometrically adjacent lines apart. Thus we need a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-invariant embedding of lines into a linear space, on which soft-argmax is well-defined. We achieve this by parametrising lines via unit-norm homogeneous vectors $\ell=(1+ρ^2)^{-1/2}(\cosθ,\sinθ,-ρ)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and applying the Veronese map $v_2(\ell)=\ell\ell^{\top}$ that satisfies $v_2(\ell)=v_2(-\ell)$. This descends continuously to an embedding of the quotient $H/\mathbb{Z}_2$ into the linear space $\mathrm{Sym}^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, where the antipodal ambiguity vanishes. Line extraction becomes a barycentre in $\mathrm{Sym}^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, projected back via its leading eigenvector. We validate our \emph{Veronese soft-argmax} in a Hough transform-based network across all resolvable lines, confirming uniform and seam-free recovery. We further derive that the $L_2$-loss on isometrically weighted Veronese embeddings equals the squared chordal distance between lines in projective space, enabling a geometrically precise training objective.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a fundamental flaw in line detection using Hough transforms: soft-argmax peak detection operates on a double-covered space (Möbius strip) that tears geometrically adjacent lines apart. The solution introduces a Veronese map embedding that converts the quotient space into a linear space where standard differentiable operations work correctly.
AI.motivation: Many vision tasks (horizon detection, fiber structure analysis) use Hough transform-based pipelines with soft-argmax for line extraction. However, soft-argmax assumes a linear space, while Hough space H = S¹ × ℝ double-covers undirected lines as a Möbius strip (since (θ,ρ) and (θ+π,-ρ) represent the same line). Operating in H tears geometrically adjacent lines apart, causing discontinuities in detection.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) Parametrize lines via unit-norm homogeneous vectors ℓ = (1+ρ²)^(-1/2)(cosθ, sinθ, -ρ) ∈ ℝ³; (2) Apply the Veronese map v₂(ℓ) = ℓℓᵀ which satisfies v₂(ℓ) = v₂(-ℓ), eliminating the ℤ₂ ambiguity; (3) This embedding descends continuously to Sym²(ℝ³), a linear space where soft-argmax becomes a meaningful barycenter; (4) Extract lines via the leading eigenvector of the barycenter; (5) Derive that L2-loss on isometrically weighted Veronese embeddings equals squared chordal distance between lines in projective space.
AI.result: Validated Veronese soft-argmax in a Hough transform-based network across all resolvable lines, confirming uniform and seam-free recovery. The method provides geometrically precise training through the derived loss function.
AI.conclusion: The Veronese map provides a mathematically rigorous solution to the geometric tearing problem in Hough transform-based line detection, enabling differentiable line extraction in a properly linearized quotient space. This approach unifies theoretical correctness with practical performance in vision pipelines.

title: ConvDeck: Conversational Paper-to-Slide Generation via Stage-Specific User Feedback
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. Project webpage: https://convdeck.github.io/
summary: Automatic academic paper-to-slide generation is inherently iterative, because creating an effective presentation requires repeated cycles of generation, critique, and revision. Recent multi-agent systems partially acknowledge this through internal critique-and-revise loops, while conversational approaches allow users to refine generated slide decks through dialog. However, these refinement processes either remain largely closed to the user or introduce feedback only after a complete deck has been produced, limiting the user's ability to participate in the iterative refinement of narrative flow, content allocation, and presentation emphasis. To address this gap, we introduce ConvDeck, a multi-agent pipeline for conversational paper-to-slide generation that distributes interaction across the pipeline through stage-specific loops, allowing users to iteratively refine both the presentation outline and the final slide deck at the stages where each kind of decision is made. These loops are driven by a refinement mechanism in which agents can think, speak, and act, enabling them to either directly apply edits or respond conversationally to clarify user feedback and discuss revision options. Our evaluation shows that stage-specific conversational feedback improves user-goal satisfaction while preserving narrative coherence, content quality, and visual presentation.

AI.tldr: ConvDeck is a multi-agent pipeline for conversational paper-to-slide generation that allows users to iteratively refine presentation outlines and slide decks through stage-specific feedback loops, improving user-goal satisfaction while maintaining narrative coherence, content quality, and visual presentation.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to automatic paper-to-slide generation have limited user participation in iterative refinement. Multi-agent systems with internal critique loops and conversational approaches either keep refinement closed to users or introduce feedback only after complete deck generation, preventing user involvement in shaping narrative flow, content allocation, and presentation emphasis.
AI.method: ConvDeck uses a multi-agent pipeline with stage-specific loops that distribute interaction across the generation process. The refinement mechanism enables agents to think, speak, and act, allowing them to either directly apply edits or engage conversationally to clarify user feedback and discuss revision options.
AI.result: Stage-specific conversational feedback improves user-goal satisfaction while preserving narrative coherence, content quality, and visual presentation.
AI.conclusion: ConvDeck demonstrates that allowing users to participate in iterative refinement at specific stages of the generation pipeline leads to better user outcomes without sacrificing the quality of the generated presentations.

title: Deterministic LLM Inference Across GPU Kernels: Power-of-Two INT8 Quantization Scales and the Limits of Tolerance-Based Conformance
comment: 9 pages (IEEEtran two-column), 3 figures, 5 tables. Fault injection against a two-stage-pinned prediction matrix (8,232 scored cells; 63-cell pre-data core, corrected and re-pinned after a disclosed smoke run); power-of-two requantization measured at 1.7B/8B/14B. Companion to arXiv:2608.13756, whose open questions on check sensitivity and deployability this paper answers
summary: Conformance suites for quantized GEMM kernels ask whether two implementations agree within a tolerance. We measure what such a suite can detect. Injecting nine faults into a reference INT8 pipeline over 8,232 layer--fault--regime cells of Qwen3-1.7B, we find that every one of five epilogue faults -- scale precision, double rounding, multiplication order, output truncation, fused ordering -- moves the output by at most a single bfloat16 spacing, and by exactly one whenever it moves it at all, across 5,880 cells. A tolerance of one spacing is therefore blind to the entire class by construction: four of the five faults are detected by no check in the suite, and the fifth only under power-of-two scales. Faults that violate the accumulator's exactness preconditions, or that break operand sharing, are detected without exception, and a null fault never fires. What a tolerance-based suite of this shape establishes is therefore narrower than interchangeability: that the preconditions hold, that operands are shared, and that differences stay within one spacing. The power-of-two constraint that exposes the one detected fault is also deployable. Requantizing every weight scale to its nearest power of two makes CUTLASS and Triton agree bitwise at every linear layer (196/196 and 252/252, against 8/196 and 10/252 under the checkpoints' own scales) and yields byte-identical generated token sequences at 1.7B, 8B and 14B (8/8 prompts, against 0/8 at all three). Observed perplexity point estimates are +0.32%, -0.28% and +0.48%; the 90% intervals cover zero at the two smaller sizes but not at 14B, reaching +0.71% and +0.76%. A previously reported +157% perplexity for this intervention was an artifact of a probe that rewrote scales without requantizing the weights; separating the effects attributes 99.8% of it to the resulting weight--scale mismatch rather than to the power-of-two constraint itself.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the effectiveness of tolerance-based conformance suites for detecting faults in quantized GEMM kernels. Through fault injection experiments on Qwen3-1.7B, the authors demonstrate that tolerance-based tests fail to detect most epilogue faults (5 out of 5), while exactness precondition violations and operand sharing violations are detected reliably. They propose requantizing weight scales to power-of-two values, which achieves bitwise agreement between CUTLASS and Triton implementations and yields byte-identical token generation across multiple model sizes.
AI.motivation: Conformance suites for quantized GEMM kernels check whether two implementations agree within a tolerance. However, it was unclear what such suites can actually detect. The authors wanted to measure the detection capabilities of tolerance-based testing approaches.
AI.method: The authors injected nine faults into a reference INT8 pipeline over 8,232 layer-fault-regime cells of Qwen3-1.7B. They tested five epilogue faults: scale precision, double rounding, multiplication order, output truncation, and fused ordering. They then proposed a practical intervention: requantizing every weight scale to its nearest power-of-two.
AI.result: Four of five epilogue faults were detected by no check in the suite, and the fifth only under power-of-two scales. Tolerance of one bfloat16 spacing is blind to the entire class by construction. Faults violating accumulator exactness preconditions or breaking operand sharing were detected without exception. Requantizing weight scales to power-of-two achieved bitwise agreement at all linear layers (196/196 for CUTLASS, 252/252 for Triton) and byte-identical generated token sequences at 1.7B, 8B, and 14B model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Tolerance-based conformance suites establish narrower guarantees than interchangeability: they verify that preconditions hold, operands are shared, and differences stay within one spacing. The power-of-two constraint is deployable and achieves perfect agreement. A previously reported +157% perplexity increase was an artifact of probe-induced weight-scale mismatch, with 99.8% of the effect attributed to this mismatch rather than the power-of-two constraint itself.

title: Hints Help But Do They Teach? Evaluating Skills Transfer in Code Generation
summary: When a hint turns a failing generated program into a passing one, does it provide missing information or merely steer the model toward a solution it could already produce? We test these hypotheses on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ using executable evaluation. For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, adaptive relevant hints rescue 36 of 79 selected failures; an unrelated hint rescues 19, while eight unhinted samples solve 46 and recover 31 of the 36 relevant-hint rescues. Phi-3.5-mini shows the same pattern: relevant hints rescue 42 of 101 failures, an unrelated hint rescues 17, and unhinted sampling solves 57, including 36 of the 42 relevant-hint rescues. Because the hint conditions use different attempt budgets, these comparisons do not isolate a purely semantic effect. Mechanistic tests on Qwen identify a stable activation direction shared by relevant and unrelated hints. Persistently adding this direction yields 14 rescues and 18 regressions, with no detectable net accuracy gain; learned low-rank interventions have a positive but imprecise estimated effect. Full textual specifications solve 22 of 24 context-defined problems, versus 5-11 for tested virtual-KV prefixes. Post-generation hidden-state probes transfer across benchmarks, with pooled AUROC 0.806 and 0.780, but their top-one selection advantage over token confidence is statistically unresolved. Overall, relevant hints can rescue failures, but most rescued solutions are already reachable through ordinary sampling, and the internal interventions tested here do not establish task-general capability transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether hints given to LLMs provide genuinely missing information or merely steer the model toward solutions it could already produce. The study tests this on code generation benchmarks (HumanEval+ and MBPP+) using executable evaluation.
AI.motivation: The core question is: when a hint helps a failing generated program pass, does it provide new information the model lacked, or does it just bias the model toward solutions it could have generated anyway? This distinction is crucial for understanding how hints work and whether they genuinely improve model capabilities.
AI.method: The researchers used executable evaluation on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks. They tested multiple conditions: (1) adaptive relevant hints, (2) unrelated hints, (3) unhinted sampling with different attempt budgets. They also conducted mechanistic tests including: identifying activation directions shared by relevant and unrelated hints, testing persistently adding this direction, and evaluating learned low-rank interventions. They tested full textual specifications vs virtual-KV prefixes, and performed post-generation hidden-state probe experiments across benchmarks.
AI.result: For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: relevant hints rescued 36/79 failures, unrelated hints rescued 19, while unhinted samples solved 46 and recovered 31 of the 36 relevant-hint rescues. For Phi-3.5-mini: relevant hints rescued 42/101 failures, unrelated hints rescued 17, and unhinted sampling solved 57, including 36 of the 42 relevant-hint rescues. Mechanistic tests identified a stable activation direction shared by relevant and unrelated hints. Adding this direction yielded 14 rescues and 18 regressions with no net accuracy gain. Full textual specifications solved 22/24 context-defined problems versus 5-11 for virtual-KV prefixes. Post-generation hidden-state probes achieved pooled AUROC of 0.806 and 0.780, but selection advantage over token confidence was statistically unresolved.
AI.conclusion: Relevant hints can rescue failures, but most rescued solutions are already reachable through ordinary sampling. The internal interventions tested (activation direction addition, low-rank interventions) do not establish task-general capability transfer. This suggests hints primarily steer the model rather than provide genuinely missing information.

title: GenScale: A Benchmark for Relative Object Scale in Image Generation and Editing
summary: Modern image generation and editing systems can produce photorealistic, prompt-aligned images, but still often render familiar objects at implausible relative sizes. To measure this failure mode, we introduce GenScale, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for real-world relative object scale in image generation and editing. GenScale contains 900 image-level entries and 1,643 pairwise anchor-target scale relations across common-object generation, human-product generation with metric dimensions, and scale correction from failed generations. We further design a human-calibrated ordinal judge for scalable pairwise scale evaluation. Last but not the least, we introduce Rescale, a model-agnostic post-processing agent for localized scale correction without modifying the source generator. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art image generators and editors cannot reliably observe relative scale yet, while Rescale consistently improves scale plausibility across generated and edited images. Together, GenScale establishes relative object scale as a distinct, measurable, and actionable capability for image generation systems.

AI.tldr: GenScale is a benchmark and evaluation protocol for measuring real-world relative object scale in image generation and editing, accompanied by Rescale, a model-agnostic post-processing agent for localized scale correction.
AI.motivation: Modern image generation and editing systems can produce photorealistic, prompt-aligned images but often render familiar objects at implausible relative sizes. This represents a distinct failure mode that lacks systematic measurement.
AI.method: The authors introduced GenScale benchmark containing 900 image-level entries and 1,643 pairwise anchor-target scale relations across three categories: common-object generation, human-product generation with metric dimensions, and scale correction from failed generations. They designed a human-calibrated ordinal judge for scalable pairwise scale evaluation, and developed Rescale as a model-agnostic post-processing agent for localized scale correction.
AI.result: Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art image generators and editors cannot reliably observe relative scale. However, Rescale consistently improves scale plausibility across generated and edited images.
AI.conclusion: GenScale establishes relative object scale as a distinct, measurable, and actionable capability for image generation systems, providing both a benchmark for evaluation and a practical solution (Rescale) for scale correction.

title: Learning What to Retain: Gated-Memory Routing for Efficient Collaboration in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems tackle complex reasoning by orchestrating how multiple agents are configured and how they collaborate. A central challenge is to adapt orchestration to the evolving collaboration state. Routing from the query alone cannot adapt to intermediate progress or errors, which hurts accuracy. Routing from the complete execution history supplies this missing context, but forces later decisions to process every prior step, including redundant or low-utility ones. This creates an execution-history overload that inflates cost. Effective orchestration instead requires a compact state that captures useful progress without accumulating redundant context. We propose Gated-Memory Routing, which conditions each decision on the query and a learned execution memory. A learned Memory Write Gate commits only non-redundant reasoning steps, and a learned Retrieval Gate supplies each agent a compact, relevant subset, so every decision conditions on a clean, informative state. At each step, the system selects the next role and backbone from this memory, while an Adaptive Halting Controller stops execution once the memory contains sufficient evidence for answering. Across five reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, our framework is both effective and efficient: it attains the best average accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.44 points, while reducing HumanEval inference cost by 31.9% relative to that baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/rajibrhasan/gated-memory-routing

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Gated-Memory Routing, a framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that uses learned memory gates to selectively store relevant reasoning steps and provide compact context for orchestration decisions, achieving better accuracy while reducing inference costs.
AI.motivation: Current LLM multi-agent systems struggle with orchestration adaptation - routing from query alone cannot adapt to intermediate progress/errors (hurting accuracy), while routing from complete execution history causes overload and cost inflation by processing redundant/low-utility steps. The goal is to find a compact state representation that captures useful progress without accumulating redundant context.
AI.method: The proposed Gated-Memory Routing framework has three key components: (1) A learned Memory Write Gate that commits only non-redundant reasoning steps to execution memory, (2) A learned Retrieval Gate that provides each agent a compact, relevant subset of memory, and (3) An Adaptive Halting Controller that stops execution once memory contains sufficient evidence. At each step, the system selects the next role and backbone from the memory.
AI.result: Across five reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, the framework achieves the best average accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.44 percentage points, while reducing HumanEval inference cost by 31.9% relative to that baseline.
AI.conclusion: Gated-Memory Routing effectively balances accuracy and efficiency in LLM-based multi-agent systems by using learned gates to maintain a compact, informative execution memory, enabling better orchestration decisions while significantly reducing computational costs.

title: Counterfactual Fragility Certificates: Exposing High-Confidence Brittleness under Structured Evidence Failure
summary: High test accuracy and good aggregate calibration do not show whether an individual prediction is structurally supported by its evidence. In tabular decision systems, failures often occur when a feature family becomes unavailable, delayed, noisy, stale, or low-trust while the model remains highly confident. Existing calibration, uncertainty, selective-prediction, explanation, and perturbation methods provide scalar scores or attribution maps, but not a recomputable audit object answering: under a declared evidence-failure protocol, what trajectory makes this prediction lose support? We introduce Counterfactual Fragility Certificates (CFC), a model-agnostic protocol-level audit certificate-not a formal robustness certificate-that maps each prediction into an ordered evidence-failure trajectory summarized by greedy flip budget, normalized margin-collapse area, degradation thresholds, and fragility dominance score. Across seven tabular benchmarks and strong linear, tree-based, boosting, and neural baselines, CFC-FDS identifies independently brittle high-confidence cases with 0.915 AUROC, improving over the strongest non-certificate score by +0.405. The advantage persists across perturbation, permutation-importance, group-SHAP, baseline-choice, seed-variance, budgeted-review, and naturalistic field-unavailability checks. Under a 20% review budget, CFC-FDS captures 88.9% of brittle high-confidence cases, compared with 31.8-37.4% for confidence and energy scores. We also evaluate fragility-aware regularization and brittleness-aware temperature correction as secondary uses. CFC provides a concrete reliability framework for exposing high-confidence brittleness missed by ordinary score-centric evaluation.

Existing methods provide scalar scores or attribution maps but lack a recomputable audit object to assess prediction fragility under evidence-failure scenarios.

The method evaluates predictions across seven tabular benchmarks using linear, tree-based, boosting, and neural baselines. Validation includes perturbation, permutation-importance, group-SHAP, baseline-choice, seed-variance, budgeted-review, and naturalistic field-unavailability checks.

It enables fragility-aware regularization and brittleness-aware temperature correction as secondary applications, offering a protocol-level audit approach beyond traditional robustness certificates.

title: Athena: Vulnerability-Affected Library Identification via Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: A single vulnerability in a widely used library can cascade through millions of dependent applications, yet more than half of vulnerability database entries contain missing or incorrect affected-library information. Existing automated approaches neglect the relational structure of vulnerability databases, treating identification as an isolated text retrieval problem. In this paper, we propose Athena, the first graph-based approach for vulnerability affected library identification. Athena models vulnerability databases as a knowledge graph and reformulates the identification problem as knowledge graph completion (KGC). It comprises three key modules: a Modeling module that constructs a security knowledge graph integrating CVEs, libraries, CWE weakness types, CPE products, and software ecosystems; a Completion module that applies a modular KGC backbone to predict missing affected libraries for a given CVE via link prediction; and a Re-ranking module that retrieves KGC candidates and rescores them using a fine-tuned LLM augmented with knowledge graph embeddings, jointly leveraging structural and textual information. Our experiments on VulLib demonstrate that Athena significantly outperforms four state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a 32% improvement in Avg. F1 over the best baseline (i.e., VulLibGen). Notably, our KGC backbone with only 110M parameters already surpasses VulLibGen's best configuration at 7B parameters, demonstrating the effectiveness of graph-based modeling; the re-ranking module then provides substantial further gains, consistently outperforming the best baseline across all evaluated LLM backbones.

AI.tldr: Athena is the first graph-based approach for identifying affected libraries in vulnerability databases. It models vulnerability data as a knowledge graph and uses knowledge graph completion (KGC) to predict missing affected libraries, significantly outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Single vulnerabilities in widely used libraries can affect millions of applications, but over half of vulnerability database entries have missing or incorrect affected-library information. Existing approaches treat identification as isolated text retrieval, ignoring the relational structure of vulnerability databases.
AI.method: Athena consists of three modules: (1) Modeling module constructing a security knowledge graph integrating CVEs, libraries, CWE weakness types, CPE products, and software ecosystems; (2) Completion module using a modular KGC backbone for link prediction to identify affected libraries for a given CVE; (3) Re-ranking module that retrieves KGC candidates and rescores them using a fine-tuned LLM augmented with knowledge graph embeddings.
AI.result: Athena achieves a 32% improvement in Avg. F1 over the best baseline (VulLibGen) on the VulLib dataset. The 110M parameter KGC backbone alone surpasses VulLibGen's 7B parameter configuration, and the re-ranking module provides further gains across all evaluated LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based modeling effectively captures the relational structure of vulnerability databases. The combination of KGC for candidate generation and LLM-based re-ranking provides a powerful approach to vulnerability affected library identification, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art text retrieval methods.
